utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked that the witness be kept out just for a minute because there were witness problems next week that I wanted to first explain to the Defence counsel and just explain to the Tribunal. The position is that of the witnesses we had hoped to call next week, only two of those originally intended for next week are now available to us, one called Mr. Whitworth, who is available on and really only on Monday. He's now a working school master in the north of England and can only get one day off and certainly one day off at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's sufficient to finish him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so. We'll do our best, and all arrangements are being made to serve his summary as soon as I can and to see him on Sunday evening and so on, and I hope to conclude him in a day. If he could be concluded in a day, other arrangements will have to be made. Kljuic comes back, I think, on Tuesday, and he's likely to be at least a day, I'm told, but we don't know how much more than a day. I then advanced up the list a witness called Jennings, who has very helpfully agreed to come earlier than he otherwise was going to come. He, I think, will come in on Wednesday, and I hope that we can deal with him on Thursday, possibly start him on Wednesday afternoon, although he won't have been seen in person until Wednesday morning. It may be that I'm not going to be able to fill the week completely with evidence because I'm not sure that there's anybody else who is going to be available simply for a small slot in next week. The important thing to draw to everyone's attention is that Jennings will be coming earlier, and I gather this is something the Defence are happy to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've had the summary of the next witness. Again, I hope it's going to be possible to get finished with his evidence this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, indeed, with the witness after him, Laustsen, who should be very short. If the next witness can be concluded in a day, that leaves half a day for Laustsen, and that should be enough. Perhaps I'm ever optimistic, but I do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're sitting tomorrow but not Friday. Yes. We've got two days left. Get on with it. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would anticipate Mr. Laustsen would not take a long time. We fully anticipate having very few, if any, questions for the next witness. As to Mr. Whitworth, he gave some substantial testimony in the Blaskic case. I don't see any reason why he should not be able to be finished in one day, provided the time is equitably arranged. With respect to Mr. Kljuic, I think one day is a good estimate. Mr. Jennings, who was not on the immediate list, we don't object to his being advanced. So long as we're given fair notice with the offer of proof or the proofing statement, that's fine with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Cerkez Defence is about on the same thinking, but we only have a problem with the witness Whitworth. We really don't think that we can finish that witness in one day, I mean both direct and cross. He is talking much about details in Vitez, and we are very much interested in that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, let's get on and see how we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May we have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so there's no mystery, the witness provided this to us overnight, and I'm putting it back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good morning. I would like to continue where we had left off yesterday with a few brief questions regarding the Viteska Brigade. Can you tell me whether at any point during your tour of duty in Bosnia, you learned anything about the size of the Viteska Brigade, that is, its manpower?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, I was never informed about the exact strength of the brigade. My estimations were at that time, and they didn't change so far, one or two thousand soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever learn any details about the organisation of the brigade, in other words, how many units they had?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption at that time was that this brigade had three or four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the soldiers of the brigade did not have their own barracks or their bases?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I never visited a really organised barracks in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see one or hear about one?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about one, and neither did I see a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You never heard that this army was working in shifts, in other words, that they were in the army or that day when they were not on duty, worked at home?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware about that. I heard about shifts, by I understood that shifts meant a duty at the front lines or other military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you collect or gather enough information to be able to provide some kind of a basic comparison with the structure of a NATO brigade as opposed to the Viteska Brigade? Or perhaps I should simplify the question. Did the brigade which you saw in Vitez, and insofar as you learned about it, remind you, by its organisation, by its strength and other elements, of a brigade which you may have as a model in NATO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reminded me of a light infantry brigade. But as I say, it was not my job, as a monitor, to gather information about military structures. I was there as a diplomat to try to establish a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I think we may agree, and you gave evidence to that effect, that in the Vitez municipality various ABiH units were operating. You mentioned some of them by their names or by their description, and we heard about some of them from other witnesses. So the only question I have of you, and you can answer it by simply "yes" or "no," did you have any knowledge of the ABiH units which I am about to mention to you? First, did you have an opportunity to notice or learn about the presence of the elements of the Busovaca Brigade? There was a detachment from Kaonik which was in the Pezici, Vranska area south, due south towards Busovaca. Did you ever see or learn about the presence of that unit in the area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not under that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you agree that in this area there were certain ABiH forces present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was more than one brigade present. I dealt with two of the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, then. You expressly mentioned 325th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They were in Kruscica. They were on the opposite side of the road, that is the northern side of the road, Tolovici, Grbavica, Preocica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to my knowledge, this brigade was split into three parts. And the third part you didn't mention was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is correct, in Stari Vitez. There was the 308th Novi Travnik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There were elements of the Jajce Brigade, which were incorporated into 325th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You never heard that significant forces, that is, parts of the Jajce Brigade, after the fall of Jajce, which took place before your arrival in Vitez, had pulled back from -- with the refugees and arrived in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about a lot of refugees coming from Jajce, but I was not aware that military units had been integrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to also learn that the 314th Brigade of the ABiH was deployed in Barin Gaj, Sljivcica area?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you wouldn't be able to identify the brigade by its name?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall the names you just mentioned. You have to point out where this brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, again, this witness has described what his function was. He's described what his knowledge was, and I wonder if we are going to be assisted by a lengthy rehearsal of the defence case about these matters. Now, no doubt, you are going to call evidence about where these various brigades were, and if we go through all that with every witness who happened to be in the valley at the time, it's going to take up an enormous amount of time. It isn't going to assist us. Now, unless there are particular matters which this witness can deal with, I suggest that we move on. His role, he's described what he was about, and it wasn't to take particular notice of divisions, brigades and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I will continue. I mean, I will change the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point during your evidence you said that the HVO at some point had refused to negotiate with Sifet Sivro, an ABiH army officer, and said that he wasn't the appropriate partner for these negotiations. Would you agree with me that in negotiations everybody wants or prefers to have an appropriate partner in order to accomplish something? This is a question of principle.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle as such is correct, but they have been negotiating with Mr. Sifet Sivro for a long time, and it struck me at one day, both in Busovaca and in Vitez, the HVO commanders refused to speak with the commanders from the other side, with whom they had been negotiating for then, I think, already two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when they were satisfied that Sivro was unable to deliver what he had promised, because his superior did not agree to what he was saying, then they changed their mind, and he was in two locations at the same time.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed about that change of mind. They just told me that they were no longer willing to negotiate with Mr. Sifet Sivro. They didn't explain to me why that was. We simply refused this request of the HVO, and later on they continued working with the same persons in the local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may ask the usher to, please, show the witness Exhibit number Z607. Perhaps we can place it on the ELMO. I believe that this was the first document introduced during the evidence of this witness. Colonel, you saw this document. You saw that this document was issued by the HVO brigade command, that is the Jure Francetic Brigade, in Zenica in April, 1993. And from the first paragraph of the first item in the decision, we see that the HOS units, which until that time, that is the time when the decision was issued, was -- parts of the ABiH army were now merged completely with the HVO. Based on this document, could you agree with me, that at least in Zenica, HOS only joined the HVO as late as April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I didn't see this document during my stay in Bosnia. I was informed about the contents and I was shown the document by Mr. Nice. I'm not aware of the exact military structures in Zenica. The only thing I learned about the HVO brigade in Zenica, that they withdrew in the direction of Grahovici when I visited that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But can you tell me whether you heard, during a briefing, or learned, found out yourself during your tour of duty in Bosnia, that in the Vitez area, that is the proper town of Vitez and the surrounding villages, another unit which people referred to as HOS was also operating?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what unit you mean to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. You yourself mentioned the Vitezovi, a special independent unit of the HVO. A lot of people refer to that unit as a HOS unit, given its previous status.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that might be true. I'm not aware of the Vitezovi being the same as the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness now, please, be shown Z1040. This document was also shown previously, and I would like to refer you to page 9, paragraph 3 on that page. The third paragraph. I will read the second sentence of it to you. "It is beyond doubt, in this area, that a war which began as a common fight against a common foe (the Serbs) has degenerated into an outright civil war." This is from a report of your organisation, ECMM, and it was drafted in June of 1993. Would you agree that if not earlier, then at least at that time, that is in mid June, your organisation did come to a conclusion that this was fundamentally a civil war that was going on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we drew that conclusion already earlier. It depends on what scale you look at it. At the scale of the municipality of, for instance, Vitez or Busovaca, it had been a civil war since April already. On a larger scale for the entire middle Bosnia, it turned into a kind of civil war as of the offensives of the 8th and 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I interrupt to make one point that it's been occurring to me to make from time to time and I haven't made it. Answers by witnesses about whether this is a civil war are not, of course, determinative of the issue, and I'm never going to examine on the point. The question of whether it's a civil war or an international armed conflict is, of course, a matter for the Chamber in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you told us that you recall that it was fairly difficult to reach Cerkez because of all the fighting and also that there were a lot of guards in front of the building where he was staying and so on and so forth. However, you managed to reach Cerkez, and this was your first working day in Vitez, and you immediately did secure a meeting with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but the meeting was organised by Mr. Friis-Pedersen who had met Cerkez already more than once before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We heard that evidence. I believe you said that while you were in this meeting with him, that some bullets had hit the window of the room where you were holding the meeting.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the same -- the window of the same room, but the building itself, the wood. They had to protect the windows. The wood was hit by several bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So those were boards which we saw in the video, which we were able to see when you spoke with Cerkez in front of that building. Does that mean that there was active fighting going on in the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of the 17th, there was fighting in some streets of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any clear idea about the ABiH forces; that is, about its organisation into brigades? Were there forces in the Vitez area similar in size, in strength, to the HVO forces, and how would you compare them to the NATO-type brigades?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them also as light infantry brigades, and the brigade in the area of Vitez was split into three parts. The total strength was also approximately between 1.000 to 2.000 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your several meetings with Mr. Cerkez, on several occasions he claimed that the major problem for maintaining the ceasefire was the ABiH troop presence -- the presence of those troops which came outside of the Vitez area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made a lot of allegations about that, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree, given the evidence we heard yesterday, that his main arguments which he used were the problem of extremists and the presence of troops from outside of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the argument he used, but that doesn't give him the right to shoot at me or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I agree, sir, but --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- block us in freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I do agree with you. My question to you is only were those the arguments he used?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the times, he used those arguments, and an extra argument was the blockade of civilians on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your main goal and the main activity went towards your efforts either to see to it that a ceasefire was reached or to maintain one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The main goal was the safety of civilians, the check on war crimes, the release of prisoners, and to be able to do that we needed a ceasefire. So the ceasefire was the first goal but not the most important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Quite. But according to your own testimony, you had to invest a great deal of effort either to win over the parties to achieve a ceasefire and to abide by a ceasefire once an agreement was reached; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In those endeavours, it follows from your testimony that you directed a great deal of time and effort into contacts with the command of the local brigade, the accused Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct for my part of the job, but there were others working on other levels and in other municipalities at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you, yourself, considered him responsible for that territory. But tell me, please, do you mean, when you refer to "territory," that he was responsible also for the part of the territory of Vitez municipality under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in view of the presence of other troops, and I think you mentioned that in passing just now, the key for the HVO side was on the other side. The headquarters were in the hotel. That is where efforts needed to focus for gaining control over all HVO units, and as a monitor, that is where you maintained your contacts, at that level? I mean your institution, as such, the ECMM, not you in person.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Thebault and Colonel Bob Stewart visited the headquarters of the operational zone every day and made the same requests as I did at the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a little about a meeting with Cerkez when you also discussed detainees, the subject of detainees. You said that there were people detained in the cinema and that they were only males and so on. Tell me, please, can we agree that Cerkez actually told you that women and children had not been detained and not, as you put it, that he had released them?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. As I recall it, he told me that they had already been released. And by asking why they were at all taken into prison, he told us that it's difficult to select soldiers and civilians taking part in the actual fighting. That's the reason why they took whole families into prison. And after a while, they found out that only the males in a certain age were a threat, and they released the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you learn, in those first few days or later, that in the cinema hall there was never a woman or child detained, that there were only men there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your visits there, were you able to gain any impression as to which unit was supervising that detention centre? Wasn't it the military police?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's hard to say. According to my memory, they were the same soldiers that protected the headquarters of the brigade, since it was in the same building. So it's hard to say whether it was another unit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during your contacts, did you ever hear that some people, at least, had gone to the cinema of their own free will, for their own safety, in view of the chaos that prevailed in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us now go on to a few questions related to Kruscica that you discussed at length. I shall be as brief as possible. In view of your testimony, we can agree that the hinterland of Kruscica, that is, the area towards the south, towards the mountains, was free, and this whole area was actually under the control of the BH army, that there was no HVO forces south of Kruscica; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see or read in BritBat reports that their Warriors had entered Kruscica on several occasions along the mountain route from the south?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that Warriors were in Kruscica several times, since I visited the town myself with Warriors. But I wasn't aware about the -- I wasn't aware of the southern route you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You always entered -- when you entered in a Warrior, you came along the main road, didn't you, going towards the south? You, yourself, never approached Kruscica from the mountain side, the roundabout way from the south?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I don't think that this mountain road was available when Kruscica was blocked. If it was, then the bridge would have told me, because it was a simultaneous effort to go into Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you are not aware of the situation regarding that southern route?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us, with respect to this access road from the main road along the valley, the main road going southwards, you tried to enter Kruscica on several occasions and were prevented by civilians. And then you discovered another road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discover it. We were told about a parallel road by the HVO themselves. And they let us use this parallel road after five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this first route going off the main road towards Kruscica was virtually inhabited for two or three kilometres along the road, there were houses, and that is where you had the problems with the civilians?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to point it out on the map, then, what road was blocked and what road appeared to be open later on, if that's of any use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the picture, generally. Yes, let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very generally, then, do you remember that this other road that the HVO told you about, that it was not inhabited, that there were only a few houses alongside the road? Do you have that picture in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you remember or not, Colonel? If you don't remember, just say so.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it matters -- the road was blocked, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter for us whether it matters. But if you don't remember, just please --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we don't want to waste too much time where a witness can't help, whereas you can call evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How about just one simple question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were both those roads indicated on the map? Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You think so? Thank you. You told us about the truck bomb in Stari Vitez. Did you ever learn later on that this was an act perpetrated by the independent HVO unit called the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We asked for an investigation and never got the results of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn or hear that as far as Cerkez is concerned, and he told you he would look into the matter, that he did inform his commander about it after having learned that the act was committed by units which were not under his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't inform us about that, and he didn't say to us that he informed his commander about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you never heard that from others, from your colleagues who had contact at the level of Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that Colonel Bob Stewart was very upset about this incident, and he never got an answer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that on the 18th of April, that is the day when the truck bomb exploded, that at the U.N. base in Nova Bila a meeting was held, and we know that it was attended on the part of the HVO by Borislav Jozic and, on behalf of the BiH Army, Refik Hajdarevic. I think that you said that you were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the same time another meeting was held, which was attended by Sifet Sivro, Sefkija Djidic, that is the commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of the BiH Army, Mario Cerkez, and some other associates of theirs; the aim being to implement the agreement on a cessation of hostilities. And that that meeting roughly lasted from about 11.00 to 17.00 hours. Did you have occasion to learn about that or to coordinate those two meetings, in view of the fact that this meeting was arranged by the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, Mr. Friis-Pederson or Mr. Landry was present at that meeting. I myself was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you can confirm that while you were attending this meeting with Jozic and Hajdarevic, there was another meeting on that same day attended by Friis-Pederson and the others whose names I have read out?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I know about this meeting in the location of BritBat. My team had separate tasks for that day, and it was, amongst others, to visit Gornji Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We can agree that the truck bomb went off sometime around 18.00 hours?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just before dawn, so in April that's -- well, I think, yeah, it's late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Later on, when you tried to investigate and you said that you went there the next day, did you hear that Sifet Sivro, Sefkija Djidic and Mario Cerkez, in other words, the local commanders of both armies, were together in a British Warrior in Stari Vitez about half an hour after the explosion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... hear that on their way back from the meeting they passed by that location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he wasn't aware of it. Now, let's move on. If he's not aware of something, there is no point pressing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on, then, to another topic. Perhaps, for the sake of explanation, I think it was a slip of the tongue, actually, on the part of my learned friend the Prosecutor. There was a question about the cinema. You were asked about civilians detained in the cinema in Dubravica, and then you confirmed that. Was there a cinema in Dubravica? I think that is a confusion. Can we agree about that? In Dubravica, civilians were detained in a school, in the gym of a school, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony that this place of detention was under the control of the already mentioned HVO units, the Vitezovi. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, my memory, they had military police insignia on their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned here a person by the name of Josip Bozic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure of that name, because I checked; there is no such name. It may be a misunderstanding, because of the language.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I wrote that name in one of my books on that day as the man who gave me a list of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your conversation attended by Mr. Buffini, you and Cerkez in front of the building, when exactly was it held? I think you said in May, but there was no more precise indication of the time.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to check it. I think it's in the middle of May somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Don't waste time. If it is the middle of May, then --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Somewhere in my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No problem. You later mentioned a meeting attended by Santic, the mayor of Vitez, Pero Skopljak as one of the political leaders, and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In hierarchical terms on the Croatian side, who was the superior? Who was the most representative of them? Who did you communicate with?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to communicate with Mr. Cerkez, but Mr. Santic as the mayor of Vitez more or less took over the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Cerkez was on the side?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my opinion, not really, because I asked him questions on military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So for military matters he was the one, and for all others Santic and Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first time that Santic and Skopljak mixed in the discussion, were present at the meetings. And it was rather confusing for me who was the one to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on. In the course of April, the beginning of May, did you receive information from the BiH Army that Muslim civilians were being detained in the Catholic church in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were allegations, I think earlier than the end of April, and that was the first time I visited the Catholic church and I spoke to the local priest. And he showed me his church, and I was convinced that there were no Muslim prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was one example of rumours and misinformation that you said more or less both sides resorted to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And we can also agree that there were never any civilians held prisoner in that church?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you have occasion to see that the roof of that church had a hole made by a shell?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that, and I wasn't attended on that by -- the priest didn't point my attention on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The church was some 100 metres from the line of separation in Stari Vitez, was it not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think a bit more than 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You referred to snipers, but I just have one question about that, because you made an assessment. Could it be said that the situation regarding the exchange of sniper fire was more or less similar in all the municipalities that you visited in this part of Central Bosnia, or were there significant differences?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both sides used snipers for occasional exchange of fire, but the occasions when we were under fire, I think most of the occasions were defined as fire coming from the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you haven't answered my question. Were there significant differences regarding sniper fire from one municipality to another?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no significant differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said briefly that you received frequent misinformation from the HVO, including Cerkez, regarding certain events at the expense of the Croats. So you would go and check, and you wouldn't always find evidence of anything having happened. You yourself went to check allegations by the HVO regarding detained Croats in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO claimed that there were Croats detained there, also in Poculica, where some of the detainees had been killed by a soldier there. Did you go to Poculica to check out that situation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked in Kruscica, and the ICRC checked in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Kruscica you were shown only one location where detainees were held, and you told us what you found there, but you were not taken to another location in Kruscica, a second location?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a second location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Remind me, please, regarding this first location that you visited. Were there several women and children there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a location in and around the school. Outside the school there was a shed. There were, I think, eight men in two small sheds, and inside the school on the top floor there were, I think, four or five women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't go west of the school, the part of the village known as Bobasi?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you, perhaps, hear within that same group of allegations that on the first day of the conflict, the 16th of April, most of the Croat inhabitants had been evacuated from Kruscica through the woods?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Also, in connection with Bobasi, one of the allegations of the HVO was that some houses had been burned down in Kruscica, and you told us that you checked and you didn't find any. And on that occasion you again, you didn't visit the part -- the western part of the village closer to Bobasi, it's a hamlet on the edge of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Mr. Cerkez asked me to check on a house still burning. He pointed out where it was. It's on the videotape. We checked that location together with the HVO liaison officer, and we couldn't find any house burning or recently been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you told on that occasion that that alleged fire was the result of acts by a special unit of the BH army called the Black Coyotes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at the meeting, Cerkez threatened to set fire to Kruscica. Didn't he say, on that occasion, that he would evacuate the civilians and set fire to Kruscica --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- or the term burned down? But it's a problem of interpretation at the meeting. Are you quite sure that he said "burned down" or "set alight" in the sense of a military jargon, implying an attack, to attack and conquer, in that sense?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I had my own interpreter with me, and she was always very clear in her English spoken language, and I wrote down the words, "I'm willing to burn down all Kruscica." So I'm sure that that's what my interpreter said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you have no note of the fact that he said, "Pull out the civilians and then burn down"?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the end, Colonel, that never happened, did it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this didn't happen. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, isn't it customary for armies to spread misinformation about each other and to spread even false threats, in view of the nature of the war such as was being waged at the time there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question, really, for the witness. Yes. Let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that at a later stage Blaskic appointed five liaison officers. Of them, one at the level of the operative zone, and four at the municipal levels, that is, brigades operating in municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it wasn't Cerkez who appointed his liaison officer and that it was done rather by his superior, Mr. Blaskic? At that time, of course.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, Mr. Jozic was appointed by Mr. Cerkez by writing and by saying, and later on Mr. Blaskic gave the order to -- I think to appoint five liaison officers. I think the one at his own level, Mr. Zarko Delic, he appointed him himself, and I'm not sure whether he appointed the other ones himself or ordered his brigade commanders to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said at some point that an HVO member, red-faced, that is how you described him and indicated him on the video, that that man threatened in Stara Bila that he would kill you if he saw you in Kruscica? You know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at the hospital, the church in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, in the hospital in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that man at that time in bed, wounded?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This happened on the 9th of June, when we evacuated the 200 people from Guca Gora, and he was outside the hospital then and threatened me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you report this, the threat, to Cerkez, as his superior, because you said you knew that he was Cerkez's man or, rather, you thought he was one of Cerkez's men?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I said it to Cerkez himself or to his liaison officer, but I'm sure I reported this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that sometime in the later half of June, the commander of the 308th Brigade of the BH army complained to you that the HVO had seized a tank of theirs and some artillery weapons. Did they mention a description of the tank and tell you which make it was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think you might have misunderstood that. The situation at, I think it was, Senkovici was that the HVO earlier gave in the lines, I think, to the Serbs, and the BiH regained these lines, I think, somewhere in the middle of June. And when they regained this ground, they captured one tank and a few artillery pieces from the BSA, so not from the HVO, and it was a T-54 tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. [Interpretation] And during this same part of the examination, you also told us how, having analysed the situation, you realised or, rather, thought that there was some cooperation between the HVO and Serbs, particularly as regards the passage of troops which were pulling out. Was it a speculation on your part or is there any report about that? That is, has it ever been confirmed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- I formed my opinion on the result of discussions with BritBat and other fellow monitors, so I didn't see it myself. BritBat recce troops went to Ovcarevo, that's northwest of Travnik, and they found a lot of evidence of Croat civilians and Croat troops withdrawn to Serb territory. And later on, the brigade commander, Mr. Leotar, commander of the brigade HVO in, I think, Guca Gora, he was sighted in Tomislavgrad a few weeks or months later on, so that's, for me, additional proof that he had found a way to go to the other side and then go to Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Still, regardless of some facts which might be pointing in that direction, neither UNPROFOR nor the ECMM, in any of the documents admitted, never mentioned that as a result of their analyses or conclusion or anything. You can't find anything about that in those documents. Am I correct or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a comment. It's not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Should I rephrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can make the comment to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No need for comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What I mean is it's the sort of matter, Mr. Kovacic, which you can put in your final submissions, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for misunderstanding, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also make your assessment about Croat hospitals, that is, hospitals controlled by Croats, and you said that they were better equipped than Bosnian hospitals or, rather, BH army hospitals. In those conversations when you enquired about hospitals, did you ever hear about preparations for war in 1991, 1992, in various Lasva Valley municipalities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Here we saw the report of your institution, ECMM, and those are fragments saying that the Nova Bila hospital was in a horrible state. You were in Nova Bila, you were in that hospital, you saw it. Could we say that that hospital was in a good state?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a kind of an emergency hospital, wartime hospital in a church. They had three surgeons and four more common doctors. They had anaesthetists, they had equipment to operation on wounded people, and if they needed anything, they would get it from us through UNHCR or through Medecins du Monde or Medecins sans Frontieres. And we actually brought a lot of equipment to them, as well as to the other side. But it was still an emergency hospital in a church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time. At several occasions when we were there, all the beds were occupied, and on some other occasions, some beds were still free.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you think that hospital was quite all right, up to the standard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you compare it to other hospitals like in Kacuni or in Kruscica or in Stari Vitez, yes, it was quite well equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there any other hospital controlled by the HVO, apart from that one? In the area, I mean.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another kind of hospital, small hospital in Busovaca, also well equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us about two events, and you said, on the basis of your account, that you thought that the army was superior to civilians in the sense that it was also responsible for uncontrollable contact of civilians. Let me remind you. You were telling us about the civilians who had blocked the road to Kruscica, and in a way you implied here that the troops or, rather, the brigade was responsible for their behaviour. Secondly, you were telling us about the meeting with the brigade commander, Grubesic, in Busovaca, and you objected to him because allegedly civilians were using civilians to dig trenches. But tell us, please, wouldn't it be a normal division that the civilian authorities be responsible for the behaviour of civilians, that is, I mean, the civilian police specifically, and on the other hand, the military authorities should bear responsibility for the behaviour of the troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I must ask you to shorten your questions. That went on for a minute and a half. You don't need to ask questions of that length.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Sir. I, indeed, wanted to summarise and to -- I probably should go step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask the witness to answer a question. Yes. Now, what was the question again, in a nutshell, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, would you agree with me that the principle governing any organised human society, that it is the civilian authorities who are responsible for the behaviour of the civilians, and the military authorities are responsible for the behaviour of soldiers, of the troops? Could we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a principle, I agree. But things go beyond that. Freedom of movement is a responsibility of the military, and if civilians obstruct that freedom of movement, then it's still the responsibility of the military to organise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is why you think that in those two cases, the army should have taken care of that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Kruscica, yes. In the case of digging trenches, that's nothing to do with freedom of movement. That's just a war crime, and war crimes shouldn't be committed by civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about the Joy Convoy which had been captured. That convoy never reached the municipality of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it reached Vitez or not. I found remains of the convoy in Novi Travnik, and I wasn't there at the time when the convoy went through the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did say so. But you said that you had heard, more or less, where it had been intercepted?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but that doesn't mean that it never reached Vitez. I think parts of it even reached Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A convoy controlled by those who were supervising the convoy while it was in total yet, in one piece, before it was attacked and captured, that convoy never reached the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I don't know whether it reached Vitez or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you are telling me about the consequences of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. Please move on now. Mr. Kovacic, you've now been cross-examining for over two hours. This witness has been subjected to more than four hours' examination by the Prosecution, two hours and a bit by your co-counsel, counsel for the co-accused, and over two hours from you. Now, I judge for myself that that really is enough. Can you try and wind up, please, within the next quarter of an hour, that is, by the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do apologise for being a little bit long, and so far I never did it so much. But you, of course, recognise that it is a very important witness for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, please get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to, please, show the witness Document Z1140,1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is a report which you signed. We saw it the day before yesterday. The date on it is the 6th of July, and I should like to draw your attention to the last paragraph, that is, item 4 on page 2. I'm referring to the story that the HVO or, rather, specifically Mario Cerkez offered a reward for cut-off parts of bodies and that an ear, a cut-off ear, had been found on an HVO prisoner. Now, from this subtitle, you heard that you took over this information from the UNPROFOR report, from the BritBat report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you did not hear anything about the sources of that information?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a daily exchange of information between BritBat and the ECMM teams working in the area, and I found it my responsibility to report this in the ECMM lines. So that's the reason why I wrote it down in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please answer my question. I understand that. You told us that. But you did not find out anything about the source about where did it reach the BritBat from? How did it get into their report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I was not in the ability to find out, since I left the day after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you try to verify that kind of information? I mean, any kind of information that you would be given, and specifically this information, did you ever verify that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally I would, but, as I told you, I write these reports in the evening, at 10.00, and I left the next morning on the 7th of July, so I wasn't able to check this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear about such incidents later on? I mean, if a reward had been offered, there must have been such cases. Have you ever heard about a similar instance about a similar case?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or before.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about it before. I heard of things like this committed by the Serb side. I never heard of it being done by the Croatian side or by the ABiH side. And, as I explained to Mr. Sayers, later on I went to Germany and the German newspapers do not report on this in that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'd like to start winding it up. Colonel, is it true that basically the whole Lasva Valley was surrounded by BiH Army forces and that then within it there were some enclaves where Croat forces had surrounded Muslim or other Bosniak troops, specifically the area of Stari Vitez, Kruscica, Poculica, Preocica, and some other smaller places? Could we agree on that general assessment?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever had opportunity, and you told us where you went after you left Bosnia, but have you ever had an opportunity to hear the final data about the civil war, I mean about the casualties and fatalities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about any specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I should like to ask you to look at yet another document. It is 1139,1, 1139,1. I should like to draw your attention to paragraph 8 on page 2. It is another of your reports of the 5th of July, so early July. And here we have three groups of your contacts, to put it in simple terms. First comes the HVO. And that, evidently, refers to Vitez. Some names are mentioned in here, Pero Skopljak, Santic. Then you evidently have the military part of the HVO, the operative zone, Blaskic, Nakic, Cerkez. So this is the military part of the contacts. And the last group under (b) is BiH, Bosnia, the Bosnian side. And here you do not have a single name. Now, how am I to interpret that? Does that mean that you had no contacts on the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I made a report on Vitez itself and I should have mentioned the ABiH elements in Vitez. The other elements were outside Vitez, so there was a separate report on elements outside Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you say Vitez, do you mean the town as such or the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you yourself said that you did have contacts with Sifet Sivro and Klestura, and you mentioned some other names, but you did not with some people?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Maybe the final part of this page is missing, I'm not sure, but it's the same order as the HVO, HDZ side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Morsink, you told us quite clearly some things you didn't know, you never heard, never had an opportunity to hear anything about. Could you tell me, if you will agree with me if I tell you, that a square, the points of which are Travnik, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Zenica, a somewhat irregular square, with Vitez roughly in its centre, and that it is about 430 kilometres square. Now, in view of your -- the number of people you had, you couldn't really cover the whole area properly, could you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning we only had one team in the Vitez area. It was my team. Later on RC Zenica was reinforced and we had a total of, I think, 15 or 16 teams; so that's 32 monitors and then the staff in Zenica itself. And later on, I think as of the middle of June, we found it enough to cover this whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, if I understand you properly, until the middle of June you had difficulty in covering the area, and you were not happy with the number of monitors?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the middle of June is the exact date, but in the beginning we had a shortage of monitors, and later on we were reinforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you believe that under circumstances as those having to control such a large area as -- at a time when so many things were taking place at one in the same time, that at that time you could really arrive at some reliable and valuable facts?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found myself able to find a lot of important facts, and the area in the beginning wasn't as large as you told me, since I only focused on Vitez and Busovaca. Travnik became important later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one question more. Yesterday there was a lot of talk about a helicopter which landed somewhere near the explosives factory in Vitez. But neither in the report, which we saw, nor you in the end, said if there were any markings on that helicopter to show that it belonged to an army.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I didn't recognise any markings on this helicopter, since it was -- the sighting was done from the British Battalion, the house at the British Battalion, and that's, I think, three or four kilometres away from the ammunition factory. And it was dawn, so I couldn't clearly see signs on the helicopter, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in relation to that factory, you and some other people called it the ammunitions factory, but, surely, you are aware that ammunition was never made there, only the explosives which, perhaps, are used, which probably are used to make ammunition?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the common way of calling this factory by the Brits, and I took over this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we shall agree that the name does not really tell us about the activity of the factory, that these two things do not correspond?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never visited this factory myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I skipped some questions, since you advised me so, and I will conclude my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one thing, Mr. Kovacic, before you sit down. You didn't cross-examine and challenge what Mr. Cerkez said on the 17th of April, that his soldiers were out of control, all the elements were out of control. Do I take it from that, that there is no dispute that that is in fact what he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We did touch that, but if you want, I could just put one straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have heard what his honour said. What exactly Cerkez said about his troops being out or under his control? His troops, did he make it precise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We asked him about our freedom of movement, the bridge being blocked by anti-tank mines, and this lorry, and the small arms fire we received at crossing the front lines. And then he made the excuse that some of his troops or some of his individual soldiers were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Under the expression "his troops," was it clear what he meant? The HVO side, so my brother, my colleague's troops, or my troops under my command? Was that clearly stated?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my memory, it was his area of responsibility. It was clearly within Vitez, the boundary of Vitez, and he never said anything or mentioned anything that it wasn't his soldiers, but under the command of somebody else. Through the interpreter, of course, he said that some of his soldiers were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you took that to mean that HVO soldiers in the territory of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it as HVO soldiers under the command of Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to remind you to ask the Colonel, when Mr. Cerkez told you that some of his men had gone out of control, was it in relation to the ceasefire or rather the violation of the ceasefire that you spoke to us about after it was established in the area? Was it to justify the violation, the non-compliance with the ceasefire? Was it in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also that, Your Honour, but in the first day there was no ceasefire and there was still firing at us. And UNPROFOR -- I was travelling in an UNPROFOR vehicle and they had the mandate by the U.N. to be able to freely move in the area, and we were blocked by allegedly soldiers led by Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the outset it had nothing to do with the ceasefire as such, but afterwards there was this ceasefire, and you requested that. And nevertheless, in spite of this ceasefire, there was still fire opened, and at that time you asked Commander Cerkez: How could it be that this fire continued despite the ceasefire? And he answered you that he could not keep control of all his men or, rather, that some of his men had escaped his control. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in conclusion, you yourself answered that the use of some weapons excluded the absence of control because certain logistics is needed if one is to use those particular weapons, and that one cannot presume the use of certain weapons without it being done under the control of higher officer of some command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And there's additional information that might clear up the situation. The first time we tried to visit Kruscica in the beginning, so I think that's the 18th of April, we had the HVO liaison officer, Mr. Boris Jozic with us, and before we entered Kruscica, he made a phone call to make sure that there was no HVO fire on Kruscica when we were there. So that points out clearly to me that there is a line of communication and that there is somebody controlling these artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to ask arising from that, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a minor point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the last thing you said, the control of artillery fire, you agreed that you did not know exactly under whose control the artillery was; was it at the level of the brigade or the operative zone? Jozic, as a member of the brigade, beyond doubt had to have had communications to the artillery, because they were part of the same army. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he called the artillery himself. He either called the brigade headquarters or the operational zone headquarters, but the result of that was that there was no fire on Kruscica during our visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it stands to reason that Jozic, a member of the brigade, and it doesn't matter who the artillery was subordinated to, that he would call for the artillery fire. It doesn't mean that he is calling his own artillery; he is calling the artillery, directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Cerkez ever explain the absence of inquiry or the results of inquiries that you sought by reference to the internal military justice system?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there ever any reference to one of the units being a home guard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said yesterday, I wasn't aware of the whole brigade being a home guard brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Cerkez ever refer you specifically to other units or to the leaders of other units as people to whom you should be addressing your inquiries and concerns?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. But he was aware of the fact that we also had contacts at the operational zone level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you make it clear, when you were speaking to him, that your interest was in the Vitez position generally?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were sniped at, were you wearing the white uniform that we can see in the photographs?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I always wore that white uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to sniping, you answered this morning that most occasions of fire came from the HVO, but there were no significant differences of sniper fire from municipalities. To clarify that, are you saying as to sniper fire that it mostly came from one side or that it was equal from both sides?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sniping fire, as such, as an exchange between two opposite parties, there was no distinction between one or the other municipality. But sniping fire aimed at us was most of the time defined as being from the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Asked about the surrounding ABiH forces yesterday and today, you yesterday said that your answer had to be seen in the context of the size of the forces or, indeed, I think the small size. Is there any further comment you want to make on that, in terms of who had the upper hand and so on?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, I also used the context of a free road to the coast. So there is a small encirclement, a larger encirclement, and then even a larger encirclement on the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kordic's position of command, did you ever have access to internal HZHB documents and orders and matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the truck bomb is concerned, it's suggested that Cerkez said it was the responsibility of other units. Had he ever identified other units to you, would you then have taken other steps and written different reports?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had made it clear to me that it wasn't his responsibility, but the responsibility of another unit, then I would have investigated that and put it in my report. On the other hand, Colonel Stewart dealt with Mr. Blaskic at a higher level about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And the same -- I needn't deal with that. We've dealt with that in general. The suggestion at the time of the threat to burn the village, he said that civilians were going to be pulled out. Had it been made clear to you that civilians were going to be pulled out of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention civilians, that they were going to be pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And had anybody done so, would that have involved different steps to be taken by you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no step for me to be taken. I could not stop foreign troops coming in, if any. It wasn't my job to stop reinforcements. It was my job to see that no war crimes or no further war crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think probably the last question. You've been asked about the reported offer of reward for ears said to have been made by Cerkez. Your original notes now being available, they having been summarised in the report, you can find them in one of your short smaller pocket books if you wish to. But for speed, is it right that the account as coming to you was detailed to the extent that ears cut off would attract 400 Deutschemarks if live, 200 Deutschemarks if dead, with a figure that I can't read, but it ends in 50 Deutschemarks for each finger. That one ear had been found and that there was -- perhaps you could interpret the rest of it. Somebody had an ear with him and there was a second HVO soldier who made the same statement.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And this soldier that had the ear with him is in a prison. I don't know in what prison, but he is in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the only other topic, question, is about Busovaca and about the position there. You said about Nakic and his reaction, but was the position in Busovaca up until July one of constant harmony or was it up and down? What was the position so far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a kind of harmony in the local joint commission. Both commanders could speak freely with each other, accompanied by their own liaison officers and sometimes the politicians. But they both spoke about a lot of casualties at the front line. So there wasn't really a reason to be satisfied. Casualties, numbers of 5 or 10 casualties each day, is too much for a local ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the commission. As to the Muslims themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, now, Mr. Nice. Time really is getting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can deal with it in another way. The other evidence on Busovaca -- yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I just want to be clear that the Colonel -- it was reported to the Colonel that somebody who was in prison did actually have an ear.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notes start at the bottom side of this page, underscored, Your Honour. Those are the notes I took when I was briefed by one of the British officers. I think it was the intelligence officer, but I'm not sure. The daily briefings at BritBat in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you read the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order of Mario Cerkez to cut off ears. Every ear, 400 D-mark." On the other side, on the other page: "50 Deutschemarks for each finger. One ear found, plus the one who did it in prison. He had the ear with him. Second HVO soldier made the same statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. Now, you are released. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness is Mr. Nihad Rebihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would like you to ask him his name and deal briefly with his background, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Your name is Nihad Rebihic, born on the 28th of August, 1949 in Preocica?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You went to a school of officers in reserve in the JNA of ex-Yugoslavia and you acquired the rank of captain, first class?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were appointed assistant secretary of the interior of Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You stayed in position until April 1990, and in May 1992, you decided to join the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were appointed coordinator of the units fighting the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the time, your commander was Commander Cengic and after that Sefkija Djidic?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict you were in Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of this conflict, your wife was killed and one of your daughters was wounded?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You left the BH Army in April 1994, and from that date onwards you were retired?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REBIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In August of that year, 1999 -- of this year, you resumed work as a teacher and you are now the principal of the school in Preocica?
